clue.text: Brass, the North-countryman might call it?

definitions.text: Brass, the North-countryman might call it?

parts.words: Brass, the North-countryman might call it?
parts.note: in northern English slang brass is money, and a blunt Northerner might describe that metal-named cash as solid, durable coin

explanation.surface: A question about what a plain-spoken man from the North of England calls brass.
explanation.walkthrough: In the North of England 'brass' is slang for money; brass is also a hard metal, so the Northerner's word for cash could be its hard sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard currency is stable money that holds its value, and brass is northern English slang for money.

clue.text: Harry unaccustomed to cooling his heels?

definitions.meaning: Harry Percy, the rebel nobleman in Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 1, known by his fiery nickname
someone who never waits about, his spurs (worn on the heels) always hot from riding

explanation.surface: A man called Harry who never likes to wait around.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cooling one's heels' means waiting idly; spurs are worn on the heels, so a man who never waits has hot spurs.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Henry Percy was nicknamed for his rashness, and the word now means any impetuous, headstrong person.

clue.text: They can be read or heard

definitions.meaning: written accounts or school assessments that are read
loud bangs, such as gunshots, that are heard

explanation.surface: A riddle about things that may be either read or listened to.
explanation.definitionFit: A written account is one sense; the other is the sharp bang of a gun going off.

clue.text: Agamemnon's captive, would you believe? Nobody did

definitions.text: Agamemnon's captive, would you believe? Nobody did

parts.words: Agamemnon's captive, would you believe? Nobody did
parts.note: the Trojan princess taken by the Greek king after Troy fell, a prophet doomed never to be believed

explanation.surface: A wry aside about a captive of the Greek king whose word no one trusted.
explanation.walkthrough: Apollo cursed this Trojan prophetess so her true predictions would never be believed; 'would you believe?' is the setter's joke on that.
explanation.definitionFit: The daughter of Priam, given to Agamemnon as war spoil, foretold disasters that nobody heeded.

clue.text: Sober fashion for judges?

indicators.note: used as a verb, to fashion is to shape anew, so the letters of sober are reshaped

explanation.surface: A remark on the sombre style of dress favoured by judges.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion' looks like a noun about style, but it is a verb telling you to reshape SOBER; the whole clue then describes judges' sober garments.
explanation.definitionFit: Judges wear long formal gowns in court, sombre garments matching their grave office.

clue.text: Auditor rebukes garden pests

parts.note: an auditor is a listener, and the ear is the organ that listens
to wig someone is an old informal word for scolding them

explanation.surface: A listener scolds the insects eating his plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Auditor' suggests an accountant, but here it is a hearer, giving EAR; 'wig' as a verb meaning scold is dated British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: These pincered insects are common nibblers of flowers and seedlings in gardens.

clue.text: Who's to blame for wild rip's entry into sect?

indicators.note: entry into means the scrambled letters go inside the word for sect

parts.note: a cult is a small religious sect

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters of rip run riot and are rearranged

parts.note: the word rip as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: A question about who is responsible for a rascal joining a religious group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' looks like it describes the rip, but it rearranges those three letters before they enter the sect's word.
explanation.definitionFit: The person to blame for a misdeed is the guilty party or offender.

clue.text: Builders could not understand why this project was abandoned

definitions.text: Builders could not understand why this project was abandoned

parts.words: Builders could not understand why this project was abandoned
parts.note: the biblical builders were given different languages so they could not understand one another, and the work stopped

explanation.surface: Puzzled builders wonder why their scheme was dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests baffled builders; in Genesis the builders literally could not understand each other once God confused their speech.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the people building a tower to reach heaven had their language confounded and gave up the work.

clue.text: One armed like four men

parts.note: four men have eight arms between them, as many as this sea creature

explanation.surface: Someone as heavily armed as a squad of four.
explanation.walkthrough: 'armed' suggests weapons, but it means having arms: four men have eight between them.
explanation.definitionFit: This sea creature has eight tentacles, the number of limbs four men share.

clue.text: He doesn't declare his takings for tax purposes

definitions.text: He doesn't declare his takings for tax purposes

parts.words: He doesn't declare his takings for tax purposes
parts.note: takings read as things taken, the loot of a thief who breaks in

explanation.surface: A trader who hides his income from the taxman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'takings' looks like a shop's earnings, but here it is stolen goods, which a housebreaker would hardly declare.
explanation.definitionFit: A housebreaker is a thief whose takings are stolen property, never reported.

clue.text: Another sound beating?

parts.note: drumming again, a second round of noisy beating

explanation.surface: Someone asks if another thorough thrashing is coming.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound beating' suggests a thrashing; read it as beating that makes a sound (drumming), and 'another' gives RE- before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An echo or reverberation is a sound coming back, and figuratively an after-effect of some event.

clue.text: Shops — a prime development? Nothing in it

indicators.note: in it means the round letter goes inside the rearranged letters
development means the letters of a prime are developed into a new order

parts.note: nothing is zero, written as the letter O

explanation.surface: A question whether shops are a promising development, with a dismissive reply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'development' rearranges A PRIME into EMPRIA, and 'in it' puts O inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Emporium is a grand word for a large store or marketplace; this is its Latin plural.

clue.text: Sort of pump one puts one's foot in?

definitions.text: Sort of pump one puts one's foot in?

parts.words: Sort of pump one puts one's foot in?
parts.note: a pump can be a shoe, but here it is a small hand pump for firefighting, steadied with a foot in a loop

explanation.surface: A question about a type of shoe you slip your foot into.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pump' suggests a slip-on shoe; the answer is the riding loop for the foot, which also names a portable water pump.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the rider's foot loop hanging from a saddle, and it names a hand-operated water pump.

clue.text: Root of perfume, topping for the dance

indicators.note: topping means cutting off the top letter of the word for the dance

parts.note: morris is a traditional English folk dance with bells and sticks

explanation.surface: A perfumer's root is crowned for the dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topping' looks like a garnish, but means beheading MORRIS. Morris dancing is a traditional English folk dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The dried root of certain irises is used as a fixative in perfumery.

clue.text: Maybe Ted is poor, but he has a bank balance

indicators.note: maybe signals the letters of Ted is poor could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Ted may be short of money, yet he holds a bank account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' rearranges TED IS POOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who puts money into a bank account holds a balance there.

clue.text: Describes the conduct of a Gilbertian Cornishman

definitions.text: Describes the conduct of a Gilbertian Cornishman

parts.words: Describes the conduct of a Gilbertian Cornishman
parts.note: a reference to the comic opera by Gilbert and Sullivan about sea-robbers from Penzance in Cornwall

explanation.surface: A word for how a character from Gilbert's Cornwall behaves.
explanation.walkthrough: W. S. Gilbert wrote the libretto of The Pirates of Penzance; Penzance is a town in Cornwall, so his Cornishmen were sea-robbers.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means behaving like a sea-robber, as the men of The Pirates of Penzance do.

clue.text: Transport taken by Nashville's president?

parts.note: Beau Nash presided over society in the spa town of Bath, where invalids were wheeled about in hooded carriages

explanation.surface: A question about how the head of a Tennessee city gets about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nashville' suggests Tennessee; read it as Nash's town, Bath, where Beau Nash was master of ceremonies. A chair is also a presiding officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A hooded wheeled chair for invalids, first popular in the English spa of Bath.

clue.text: A unit is deployed in North Africa

indicators.note: deployed, as troops are moved into new positions, means these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A military unit is sent to North Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deployed' rearranges A UNIT IS; 'is' belongs to the letters, not the indicator.
explanation.definitionFit: The country is a part of North Africa, lying on the Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Rome can be destroyed as an Italian city

indicators.note: be destroyed means the letters of Rome can are broken up and remade

explanation.surface: Rome can fall, as one more city of Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'be destroyed' rearranges ROME CAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in Lombardy, famed for violin makers such as Stradivari.

clue.text: Sounds like something owed for a good buy, say

indicators.note: sounds like means the words for something owed are heard as another word

parts.note: a due, as in a debt or payment owed

explanation.surface: A remark on paying what you owe after getting a bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good buy, say' is itself heard as goodbye, the definition; 'say' marks it as a sound-alike example.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word is a farewell, which spoken English renders as goodbye.

clue.text: Miss Heath identifies herself with the New World

parts.note: a woman introducing herself says I am, giving the verb
Erica is the botanical genus of heath plants and also a girl's name

explanation.surface: A Miss Heath declares she represents the Americas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Miss Heath' looks like a surname; Erica is the Latin name of heather and a woman's name, so she says 'am Erica'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Americas were called the New World by Europeans who found them after Columbus.

clue.text: Not exactly what the weatherman means by 26

definitions.text: Not exactly what the weatherman means by 26

parts.words: Not exactly what the weatherman means by 26
parts.note: entry 26 is gym equipment of two non-meeting rails; the forecaster's lines of equal pressure never meet either

explanation.surface: A forecaster uses a word from another clue in a different sense.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines of equal pressure on a weather map never cross, like the two rails of the gym apparatus at 26, hence 'not exactly'.
explanation.definitionFit: These are lines on a weather chart joining places of equal atmospheric pressure.

clue.text: Those fleeing these hazards

definitions.meaning: people who do a bunk, British slang for running away
sand-filled hollows on a golf course

explanation.surface: People running from dangers ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'do a bunk' is British slang for absconding; the golf sense is sand traps.
explanation.definitionFit: Absconders are those who scarper; the other sense is the sand traps that golfers dread.

clue.text: Charming way to read letters

parts.note: a magic charm is one sense, and naming the letters of a word one by one is another

explanation.surface: A delightful method of reading correspondence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charming' looks like praise but points to magic; 'read letters' means name them one by one.
explanation.definitionFit: It means an enchantment or incantation, and also to name a word's letters in order.

clue.text: They're no great shakes

parts.note: the idiom for something unimpressive, read literally as small shakings of the ground

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark about some mediocre people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No great shakes' means unimpressive; literally, minor shakes are slight quakes.
explanation.definitionFit: These are slight quivers or minor earthquakes, small shakings rather than great ones.

clue.text: To be flexible, money is not all

parts.note: L stands for the pound, from Latin libra, the British unit of money
some means a part rather than all

explanation.surface: A maxim that being adaptable matters more than wealth.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the old abbreviation for a pound sterling (libra).
explanation.definitionFit: The word means supple and lithe, able to bend gracefully.

clue.text: Where Americans give elegance a try

parts.note: chic means stylish elegance
to have a go is to make an attempt

explanation.surface: Americans are said to give smartness a chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'give' is the link; the definition is a place where Americans live.
explanation.definitionFit: The Windy City in Illinois is a place where many Americans live.

clue.text: They don't meet for drinks in the gymnasium

definitions.text: They don't meet for drinks in the gymnasium

parts.words: They don't meet for drinks in the gymnasium
parts.note: lines that never meet, plus counters where drinks are served, together naming two rails of gym apparatus

explanation.surface: People who never go out for drinks together at the gym.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests people avoiding a social drink; read as two rails that never meet, plus places for drinks, it names the gymnastics apparatus.
explanation.definitionFit: This gymnastic apparatus has two raised rails running side by side at a constant distance.
